caption:
Google will switch off Gemini, NotebookLM and Search for K-12 student accounts by default in early 2027.
Schools can turn them back on. But a school that blocks AI entirely loses Google Search too.
Google says Search and AI are now too deeply integrated to split.

Should schools have to choose between AI and Google Search?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: Chalkbeat · Photo: John Moore / Getty Images, Techaeris, Anadolu via Getty Images
threads_text: Google will turn off Gemini and Search for K-12 student accounts by default in early 2027. The catch: a school that wants no AI at all also loses Google Search, because Google says the two can't be separated. Is that a fair choice to hand schools?

slides.headline: Google just told schools: turn off our AI and you *lose Google Search*

site_article.headline: Google will turn off AI for K-12 students by default, but schools that refuse AI lose Search
site_article.dek: Starting in early 2027, administrators must switch on Gemini, NotebookLM and Search, and Google says Search cannot be offered without its AI features.
site_article.summary: Google said on November 3, 2026 that Gemini, NotebookLM and Google Search will be off by default for school-managed K-12 student accounts starting in early 2027. Schools that want no AI at all will have to give up Google Search, because the company says the two are integrated.
site_article.seo_title: Google makes school AI opt-in, but no AI means no Search
site_article.seo_description: From early 2027, Gemini and Search are off by default for K-12 student accounts. Schools that block AI entirely also lose Google Search.
site_article.answer_summary: Schools can switch off Google's AI for K-12 students starting in early 2027, but they cannot keep Google Search without its AI features. A school that turns AI off entirely loses Search as well.
site_article.hero_alt: A row of open laptops on classroom desks, chained together with a padlock, in front of a Google logo on a wall.

paragraphs.text: Google announced on November 3, 2026 that Gemini, NotebookLM and Google Search will be switched off by default for school-managed K-12 student accounts starting in early 2027. School administrators will have to turn the products on before students can use them, according to Forbes and CNN.

The change reverses a decision Google made in August, when it turned Gemini on by default for students in Google Classroom, CNN reported. Chalkbeat, citing Education Week, said that earlier switch caught many districts off guard.

The new controls come with a condition. Schools cannot keep conventional Google Search while removing only AI Overviews, the AI summaries that appear above search results. A district that wants no AI on student accounts has to turn off Google Search entirely, and students will see a message saying Search is not available, according to CNN.

Chris Phillips, Google's vice president and general manager of education, told Forbes that "Search and AI are deeply integrated." Speaking to Chalkbeat, he said that a school that simply wants AI off has the choice to not have Search on at all.

Techaeris reported that the Los Angeles Unified School District said in September that it hoped students could search with AI Overviews switched off, and that Google did not offer that option. Districts that do allow AI will get two search modes in early 2027: standard Search with AI Overviews and AI chats, or Search routed through a tutoring mode called Guided Learning.

Google also began rolling out Guided Learning in Google Classroom on November 3 for schools that have already enabled Gemini. The mode asks questions and walks students through problems instead of handing over answers. Students cannot switch it off within those activities, and teachers can assign work through it and review the chats to see how students approached a problem, according to Forbes and Chalkbeat.

A version of Guided Learning inside AI Overviews will be tested with a small group of US schools in November before a wider rollout early in the new year, Chalkbeat reported. When Search detects a homework question, students will be prompted to work through it step by step, according to CNN.

Google pointed to early research to support the approach. In a preliminary randomized trial at the University of Tokyo, students using Guided Learning raised their test scores by 8.1 percentage points, compared with 5.3 points for students using conventional online resources. Forbes noted that the study covered only half a day of independent study and that its full report had not yet been published.

The changes follow a broad backlash against AI in classrooms. Large districts including New York City and Los Angeles have restricted student use of generative AI tools, and parents have pushed for more control over how children use technology at school, according to CNN and Chalkbeat. Google's Chromebooks are used by tens of millions of students, CNN reported.

Common Sense Media rates the AI Overviews and AI Mode features in Google Search as an unacceptable risk for students, Chalkbeat reported. Eisha Bush, the group's head of teaching and learning, told Chalkbeat that the likelihood of schools and students avoiding Google Search is "really slim to none."

Google said the changes respond to calls from educators and policymakers for more control over AI tools. Phillips wrote that the company will share more details with schools in the coming months, before the new defaults take effect.

In practice, the opt-out is narrow. Search is so central to schoolwork that few districts are likely to turn it off, which means most students will keep seeing AI in their results. The real choice for schools is less about whether students meet Google's AI and more about which version of it they meet: the standard one or the tutoring mode.

The next signal is how Google's promised administrator controls work when it publishes the details in the coming months, and whether large districts such as Los Angeles accept Search with AI or look for other options before the defaults change in early 2027.
